stem: Which pest of maize has the scientific name *Busseola fusca*?

options.content: Maize stalk borer
options.rationale: Correct: its larvae tunnel inside maize and sorghum stems.

options.content: Fall armyworm
options.rationale: Fall armyworm is *Spodoptera frugiperda*.

options.content: American bollworm
options.rationale: The American bollworm is *Helicoverpa armigera*.

options.content: Maize weevil
options.rationale: Weevils are beetles that attack stored grain, not stems.

explanation: *Busseola fusca* is the maize stalk borer, a moth whose caterpillars feed in the funnel and then bore into the stem.

stem: Why must a farmer buy new hybrid maize seed every season instead of saving seed from the crop?

options.content: Saved seed gives uneven plants with lower yields
options.rationale: Correct: the F1 uniformity and hybrid vigour are lost in the next generation.

options.content: Hybrid seed cannot germinate once it has been stored
options.rationale: Hybrid grain germinates; the problem is how the plants perform.

options.content: Saving seed from a hybrid crop is banned by the GMB
options.rationale: This is not the reason; the reason is biological.

options.content: Hybrid plants produce cobs that contain no viable seed
options.rationale: Hybrid cobs contain viable grain.

explanation: A hybrid is the F1 of two inbred lines. Its offspring segregate, so the next crop is variable and yields fall.

stem: Which sign shows that maize grain has reached physiological maturity?

options.content: Silks appear at the tips of the young cobs
options.rationale: Silking happens at flowering, months before maturity.

options.content: Tassels appear at the top of each plant
options.rationale: Tasselling is the start of flowering.

options.content: A black layer forms at the base of each kernel
options.rationale: Correct: the grain has reached its maximum dry mass.

options.content: The upper leaves turn a dark, glossy green and curl
options.rationale: Leaves dry and turn brown at maturity.

explanation: The black layer is a dark band where the kernel joins the cob; after it forms the grain only loses water.

stem: A farmer in natural region IV receives the first effective rains in mid-December. Which maize cultivar is the best choice?

options.content: A late-maturing (long-season) cultivar
options.rationale: It needs a long, wet season and would face drought at grain filling.

options.content: Any cultivar, because maturity group has no effect
options.rationale: Maturity group is the main choice for a short season.

options.content: Grain saved from last season's hybrid crop
options.rationale: Saved hybrid seed gives uneven, lower-yielding plants.

options.content: An early-maturing (short-season) cultivar
options.rationale: Correct: it can finish before the short, unreliable season ends.

explanation: Late planting in a dry region leaves a short season, so an early cultivar reduces the risk of drought at tasselling and grain fill.
hints: How long is the growing season left after mid-December in a dry region?

stem: Which insects spread maize streak virus?

options.content: Aphids
options.rationale: Aphids spread many viruses, but maize streak virus is spread by leafhoppers.

options.content: Leafhoppers
options.rationale: Correct: they carry the virus from infected grasses and maize.

options.content: Grain weevils
options.rationale: Weevils attack stored grain.

options.content: Termites
options.rationale: Termites damage roots and stems; they do not carry this virus.

explanation: Leafhoppers transmit maize streak virus; control includes resistant cultivars and removing grass weeds.

stem: Where should Compound D be placed when it is applied at planting?

options.content: In direct contact with the seed so roots find it at once
options.rationale: Concentrated salts touching the seed can scorch it and spoil germination.

options.content: On the leaves of the young plants after emergence
options.rationale: Basal fertiliser goes in the soil at planting.

options.content: On the soil surface between the rows after harvest
options.rationale: After harvest the fertiliser cannot help the crop.

options.content: In the furrow or hole a few centimetres from the seed
options.rationale: Correct: close enough for young roots, but not touching the seed.

explanation: Basal fertiliser is banded or placed near the seed so the phosphorus is near the young roots without burning the seed.
hints: Fertiliser salts draw water out of seeds.

stem: Which observation best shows that young maize is being attacked by fall armyworm rather than stalk borer?

options.content: Narrow yellow streaks running along the length of the leaves
options.rationale: These are signs of maize streak virus.

options.content: Ragged holes and heaps of sawdust-like droppings in the funnel
options.rationale: Correct: fall armyworm feeds openly in the whorl and leaves frass.

options.content: Grey rectangular spots between the leaf veins
options.rationale: These are signs of grey leaf spot, a fungal disease.

options.content: Small round holes in stored grain with fine powder left in the bag
options.rationale: These are signs of weevils in storage.

explanation: Fall armyworm caterpillars feed in the funnel, leaving ragged holes and frass; stalk borer causes windowing and tunnels inside the stem.
hints: Think of where each larva feeds.

stem: Why does maize planted three weeks after the first effective rains usually yield less than maize planted with them?

options.content: Late-planted maize cannot take up any fertiliser at all
options.rationale: Late maize still takes up fertiliser.

options.content: Seed loses all its viability if it is stored until late December
options.rationale: Seed stays viable for this time if stored well.

options.content: It has a shorter season and is more likely to meet drought at grain fill
options.rationale: Correct: the crop loses growing time and the late rains may stop.

options.content: Late-planted maize is never attacked by stalk borer or by leafhoppers at all
options.rationale: Late plantings often suffer more pests, not fewer.

explanation: Late planting shortens the season, nitrogen released early in the rains is leached, and later crops often suffer more pests such as leafhoppers and armyworm.
hints: Count the growing days left before the rains end.

stem: Maize is a frost-tolerant crop that can be planted safely in winter.
explanation: False. Maize is killed by frost and is a summer (rain-season) crop in Zimbabwe; wheat is the winter cereal.

stem: Maize grain stored at a high moisture content is likely to go mouldy and be attacked by insects.
explanation: True. Grain is dried to about 12.5% moisture before storage because damp grain heats, moulds and favours insects.

stem: Match each maize problem with its cause.

left.content: Holes and powder in stored grain

explanation: Know each problem's cause: virus, fungus, insect or nutrient shortage.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Maize is top dressed with {{blank:a}} nitrate, which supplies the nutrient {{blank:b}}, usually in split doses.

explanation: Ammonium nitrate (about 34.5% N) is the usual top dressing for maize.

stem: Maize is planted at 75 cm × 25 cm with one plant per station. Calculate the plant population per hectare, to the nearest whole plant.
explanation: Area per station = 0.75 m × 0.25 m = 0.1875 m². Plants/ha = 10,000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53,333. Using centimetres without converting (75 × 25 = 1,875) gives a meaningless answer.
workedSolution: 1. Area per station = 0.75 m × 0.25 m = 0.1875 m². Plants/ha = 10,000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53,333. Using centimetres without converting (75 × 25 = 1,875) gives a meaningless answer.

stem: Chipo will apply Compound D at 350 kg/ha to 0.8 ha of maize. Fertiliser is sold in 50 kg bags. Calculate the number of bags she must buy. Round UP to whole bags.
explanation: Mass = 350 × 0.8 = 280 kg; 280 ÷ 50 = 5.6 bags, so she buys 6. Rounding down to 5 would leave part of the field without fertiliser.
workedSolution:
1. Mass needed = 350 kg/ha × 0.8 ha = 280 kg.
2. Bags = 280 ÷ 50 = 5.6.
3. Round up: 6 bags.
hints: Divide by the bag size and round up.

stem: Maize at 75 cm × 25 cm (one plant per station) is to be top dressed with ammonium nitrate at 150 kg/ha. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate to give each plant, in g, to one decimal place.
explanation: Plants/ha = 10,000 ÷ (0.75 × 0.25) = 53,333. 150 kg = 150,000 g; 150,000 ÷ 53,333 = 2.81 g, which is 2.8 g per plant. Forgetting to change kg to g gives a tiny, wrong answer.
hints: First find the number of plants per hectare.
Convert kg to g before dividing.

stem: Farai harvested 2,880 kg of dry maize grain from 0.6 ha. Calculate his yield in t/ha.
explanation: 2,880 ÷ 0.6 = 4800 kg/ha = 4.8 t/ha. Multiplying by the area instead of dividing gives 1.728, which is wrong.
workedSolution: 1. 2,880 ÷ 0.6 = 4800 kg/ha = 4.8 t/ha. Multiplying by the area instead of dividing gives 1.728, which is wrong.

stem: Name the parasitic weed that attaches to the roots of maize and sorghum on poor, sandy soils.
explanation: **Witchweed** (*Striga*) is a root parasite of maize, sorghum and millets.

stem: Explain why weeds must be controlled in maize during the first six to eight weeks after emergence.

points.description: Weeds compete with young maize for water, nutrients (especially nitrogen) and light.
Young maize grows slowly and is easily shaded or starved, so early competition causes the largest yield loss.
Once the canopy closes the maize shades out later weeds (and weeds also harbour pests such as leafhoppers).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In the first weeks the maize is small and grows slowly, so weeds take water, nitrogen and light from it and the yield falls most. After about eight weeks the maize canopy shades the ground and later weeds do much less harm.

explanation: Critical period of weed competition.
hints: What do weeds and young maize compete for?

stem: Describe how Nyasha should prepare and store her shelled maize grain so that it keeps safely until the next harvest.

points.description: Dry the grain to a safe moisture content (about 12.5%), e.g. on a clean floor or tarpaulin in the sun.
Clean the grain (remove broken grain, chaff and dirt) and clean the store of old grain and insects.
Treat the grain with an approved storage protectant or store it in hermetic (airtight) bags.
Keep bags on pallets off the floor, away from walls, in a dry, cool, rat-proof store, and inspect regularly.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nyasha should dry the grain to about 12.5% moisture and clean it. She should clean and repair the store, treat the grain with an approved protectant or use hermetic bags, and stack the bags on pallets away from walls in a dry, rat-proof store, checking them often for weevils and mould.

explanation: Dry, clean, protect, store properly, inspect.
hints: Think of moisture, insects, rodents and the store itself.

stem:
Form 4 pupils at a school near Marondera grew the same hybrid on three 200 m² plots at different spacings and recorded the grain harvested.

| Plot | Spacing (cm) | Plants per station | Grain harvested from the 200 m² plot (kg) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 90 × 30 | 1 | 98 |
| B | 75 × 25 | 1 | 112 |
| C | 75 × 20 | 1 | 104 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the plant population per hectare in plot C, to the nearest whole plant.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the yield of plot B in t/ha.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which plot gave the highest yield per hectare?

options.content: Plot A
options.rationale: Plot A gave 4.9 t/ha.

options.content: Plot C
options.rationale: Plot C gave 5.2 t/ha.

options.content: Plot B
options.rationale: Correct: 5.6 t/ha.

options.content: All three plots gave the same yield
options.rationale: Equal plots, different masses: the yields differ.

parts.explanation: The plots are the same size, so the largest harvest (112 kg) is the highest yield: B 5.6, C 5.2, A 4.9 t/ha.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Plot C had the most plants but a lower yield than plot B. Explain why.

points.description: Crowded plants compete strongly for water, nutrients and light.
So each plant forms smaller cobs, or some plants are barren / thin stems lodge.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest why a farmer in a drier area might choose the spacing used in plot A.

points.description: Fewer plants per hectare share the limited soil water, so each plant is less likely to wilt and fail.

explanation: Calculate plant population and yield, then explain how spacing affects yield.
hints: Plants/ha = 10,000 ÷ (row spacing in m × in-row spacing in m).

stem:
In January, Farai scouts three maize fields near Gokwe for fall armyworm by checking plants at several places in each field.

| Field | Plants checked | Plants with fresh funnel damage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Field 1 | 50 | 4 |
| Field 2 | 50 | 14 |
| Field 3 | 50 | 9 |

Assume his extension officer advises that a field should be treated when more than 20% of the young plants show fresh damage.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of plants with fresh damage in Field 2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which field or fields should be treated now, according to the advice?

options.content: Fields 2 and 3
options.rationale: Field 3 is at 18%, below the threshold.

options.content: All three fields
options.rationale: Fields 1 (8%) and 3 (18%) are below 20%.

options.content: None of the fields
options.rationale: Field 2 is above the threshold.

options.content: Field 2 only
options.rationale: Correct: only Field 2 (28%) is above 20%.

parts.explanation: Field 1 = 8%, Field 2 = 28%, Field 3 = 18%; only Field 2 exceeds 20%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** signs Farai would look for when scouting.

points.description: Ragged holes / windowing on young leaves.
Moist sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the funnel / caterpillars in the funnel.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why scouting and a threshold are better than spraying every field every week.

points.description: Spraying only when damage is high enough to cause yield loss saves money on chemicals and labour.
Fewer sprays protect natural enemies (parasitoids, predators) that help control the pest.
Fewer sprays slow the development of insecticide resistance and reduce risks to people and the environment.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe **three** non-chemical methods Farai could use to reduce fall armyworm damage next season.

points.description: Plant early and at the same time as neighbours so the crop is past the most vulnerable stage.
Hand-pick and crush egg masses and caterpillars / apply ash or sand in the funnel.
Rotate or intercrop with legumes, keep fields weed-free and destroy crop residues; encourage natural enemies.

explanation: Use scouting data and a threshold to decide on control, then describe integrated fall armyworm management.
hints: Compare each field with the threshold.

stem: Thandeka will plant maize at 90 cm × 25 cm, one plant per station. A germination test shows 85% of the seed germinates, and 1,000 seeds have a mass of 280 g.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of plants per hectare, to the nearest whole plant.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the minimum mass of seed needed per hectare, in kg, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Seeds = 44,444 ÷ 0.85 = 52,288; mass = 52,288 × 0.28 g = 14,641 g ≈ 14.6 kg/ha. Ignoring germination gives 12.4 kg; multiplying by 0.85 instead of dividing gives 10.6 kg.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Seeds = 44,444 ÷ 0.85 = 52,288; mass = 52,288 × 0.28 g = 14,641 g ≈ 14.6 kg/ha. Ignoring germination gives 12.4 kg; multiplying by 0.85 instead of dividing gives 10.6 kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why farmers usually sow more seed than this minimum.

points.description: Some seeds or seedlings are lost to pests (cutworms, birds, rodents) and diseases or poor seedbed conditions.
Sowing two seeds per station and thinning to one ensures every station has a plant, so the population is not reduced by gaps.

explanation: Plant population and seed rate allowing for germination.
